name: Nebraska

notes: Food for home, candy and soft drinks included, is exempt from the state and local taxes; prepared food and vending-machine food are taxed.
Alcohol is taxed at the sales tax rate, on top of gallonage taxes left out here: beer 31 cents a gallon, wine 95 cents, spirits $3.75.

Cigarettes and other tobacco are taxed at the sales tax rate, on top of excise taxes left out here: 64 cents a pack of cigarettes, 20% of the price on other tobacco (snuff 44 cents an ounce), and vapor products 5 cents a milliliter or 10%.
Household supplies: diapers are taxed in full until they become exempt on July 1, 2027.
Personal care products: menstrual products are exempt, which is not taken out here.
Barber and beauty services aren't taxed (they aren't on the statute's list of taxable services).
Clothing is taxed in full; Nebraska has no sales tax holiday.
Laundry and dry cleaning aren't taxed.
Motor fuel is exempt from the sales tax and pays 31.8 cents a gallon (July 1 to December 31, 2026) plus a 0.9-cent release fee instead, left out here.
Repair labor isn't taxed when it is stated separately; parts are taxed.
City occupation taxes on restaurants are counted where the city gives the rate (the local rates table names them); restaurants show them on the bill with the sales tax charged on top.
Hotel stays pay the sales tax plus a 1% state lodging tax, a county lodging tax (4% in most counties) and some cities' hotel occupation taxes; not counted here.
The services below are from Neb. Rev. Stat. 77-2701.16 and the Department of Revenue's guides.
gaps: Local rate in each city is the most common among its address records. Dakota County's 0.5% county tax applies only outside cities and villages with their own tax, and is included there.

Good Life districts: only retailers that opted in within Omaha's Avenue One district charge a lower state rate (2.75% instead of 5.5%); not reflected here. The other districts (Nebraska Crossing in Gretna, Grand Island, La Belle Vue in Bellevue and Kearney) charge the full rate.

City occupation taxes on restaurants are counted in the restaurant rate where the city's own page or code gives the rate (Omaha and Ralston 2.5%; Lincoln, Norfolk and Fremont 2%, Fremont's from November 1, 2026; Grand Island 1.5%; Kearney and La Vista 1%). Ralston's and La Vista's stop for the rest of a fiscal year once they raise $700,000. Hotel stays pay a 1% state lodging tax, most counties' 4% lodging tax and some cities' hotel occupation taxes, which aren't counted.

Rate changes on January 1, 2027 (Eagle and Hay Springs to 1.5%, Winside's new 1%) and the November 3, 2026 votes (Fremont, Imperial, Clearwater, Yutan, Chappell, Big Springs, La Vista) aren't in the rates; each is noted on its page.

3103950: The La Belle Vue Good Life District here charges the full state rate (Department of Revenue).
3104895: Big Springs' voters decide on November 3, 2026 on keeping its 1% local sales tax with no end date (as reported); the current rate would be used here.
Big Springs is less than half of each census tract it is in, so the figures here use the surrounding area's rates for its tract, not its own.
3108885: Chappell's voters decide on November 3, 2026 on continuing a 0.5% part of its local sales tax from April 1, 2028 to March 31, 2039 (as reported); the current rate would be used here.
Chappell is less than half of each census tract it is in, so the figures here use the surrounding area's rates for its tract, not its own.
3109445: Clearwater's voters decide on November 3, 2026 on raising its local sales tax from 1.5% to 2% from July 1, 2027 to September 30, 2036 (as reported); the current rate would be used here.
Clearwater is less than half of each census tract it is in, so the figures here use the surrounding area's rates for its tract, not its own.
3114100: Eagle's local rate rises from 1% to 1.5% on January 1, 2027 (Department of Revenue); the current rate would be used here.
Eagle is less than half of each census tract it is in, so the figures here use the surrounding area's rates for its tract, not its own.
3117670: Fremont's occupation tax on food and nonalcoholic drinks at restaurants is counted in its restaurant rate: 2%, its rate from November 1, 2026 (1% before; Ordinance 5756, City of Fremont).
Fremont's voters decide on November 3, 2026 on raising its local sales tax from 1.5% to 2% (as reported); the current rate is used here.
3119595: Grand Island's 1.5% occupation tax on food and drink sold by restaurants, bars, food trucks and stands (alcohol included since July 1, 2016) is counted in its restaurant rate (Ordinance 9588; City of Grand Island).
Grand Island's Good Life District charges the full state rate (Department of Revenue).
3120260: The Nebraska Crossing Good Life District here charges the full state rate (Department of Revenue).
3121730: Hay Springs' local rate rises from 1% to 1.5% on January 1, 2027 (Department of Revenue); the current rate would be used here.
Hay Springs is less than half of each census tract it is in, so the figures here use the surrounding area's rates for its tract, not its own.
3123690: Imperial's voters decide on November 3, 2026 on keeping its 1% local sales tax with no end date and, in a second question, on adding 0.5% (as reported); the current rate would be used here.
Imperial is less than half of each census tract it is in, so the figures here use the surrounding area's rates for its tract, not its own.
3125055: Kearney's 1% occupation tax on food and nonalcoholic drinks sold by restaurants and drinking places (alcohol isn't taxed), in place until January 31, 2042, is counted in its restaurant rate (City of Kearney). Its 2% hotel occupation tax and the 1% occupation taxes on all sales in its two enhanced employment areas aren't counted.
Kearney's Good Life District charges the full state rate (Department of Revenue).
3126385: La Vista's 1% occupation tax on restaurants is counted in its restaurant rate (City of La Vista); the city caps what it collects at $700,000 a year. Its 5% hotel occupation tax isn't counted. On November 3, 2026 La Vista voters decide on replacing it with a fixed 2.5% tax (City of La Vista ballot language); the current 1% is used here.
3128000: Lincoln's 2% occupation tax on restaurants and bars (food and drink subject to sales tax) is counted in its restaurant rate (City of Lincoln). Lincoln also levies 4% on hotel rooms, short-term rentals and car rentals, and occupation taxes on all sales in two shopping areas (Gateway 0.5%, SouthPointe Pavilions 1%), which aren't counted.
3134615: Norfolk's 2% occupation tax on restaurants and drinking places, in place since February 1, 2011, is counted in its restaurant rate (City Code 13-183).
3137000: Omaha's 2.5% occupation tax on food and drink prepared for immediate consumption (restaurants, bars, caterers, food trucks and grocery and convenience-store food counters), in place since October 1, 2010, is counted in its restaurant rate (Omaha Municipal Code ch. 19, art. XVI; City of Omaha).
In Omaha's Avenue One Good Life District, retailers that opted in charge a 2.75% state rate instead of 5.5% (Department of Revenue); not reflected here.
3140605: Ralston's 2.5% occupation tax on restaurants and drinking places, in place since November 1, 2015, is counted in its restaurant rate (Municipal Code 10-1703). The tax is suspended for the rest of the fiscal year once it has raised $700,000, so late in some years it may not be charged.
3153380: Winside starts a 1% local sales tax on January 1, 2027 (Department of Revenue); it isn't in the rates here.
3154115: Yutan's voters decide on November 3, 2026 on a new 1.5% local sales tax (as reported); it isn't in the rates here.

programs: Tax increment financing projects are mapped for Omaha (active projects, and the four Urban Core Housing and Mobility districts of 2022), with Omaha's nine business improvement districts, Lincoln's seven neighborhood maintenance business improvement districts, Hastings' downtown district, the enterprise zones (Omaha, South Sioux City and Otoe County) and the Innovation Hub tracts.
